claim: A genome-wide genetic screen in Drosophila identified 360 genes that potentially interact with Notch to influence proliferation.
source: We performed a genome-wide screen for modifiers of an activated Notch (Nact)-induced large eye phenotype to uncover novel genes that interact with Notch to affect proliferation using the Exelixis collection of insertional mutations, which covers approximately 50% of the genome (Thibault et al., 2004; Kankel et al., 2007; Pallavi et al., 2012). We screened for enhancement or suppression of the large eye phenotype (Figure 1A). As a result, we identified 360 Drosophila genes that are predicted to affect Notch-induced proliferation in the eye
evidence: The screen methodology and results are described in the text, with the number of identified genes explicitly stated.

claim: 206 of the 360 identified genes have clear human orthologs.
source: of particular interest are the 206 genes that have clear human orthologs (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The number of genes with human orthologs is stated and referenced to supplementary data.

claim: 42 GO categories are significantly enriched among the 360 identified genes.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis reveals that 42 GO categories are significantly enriched among the 360 genes (Figure 1B, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: GO enrichment analysis results are presented with reference to figure and supplementary data.

claim: The enriched GO terms fall into three broad categories: genes involved in morphogenesis and development, genes involved in cell division and the cell cycle, and genes involved in transcription.
source: The majority of these enriched GO terms fall into three broad categories: genes involved in morphogenesis and development, genes involved in cell division and the cell cycle, and genes involved in transcription.
evidence: The categorization of enriched GO terms is explicitly stated based on the analysis.

claim: 84 of the 360 genes did not have any associated GO or INTERPRO annotation.
source: Notably, 84 of the 360 genes did not have any associated GO or INTERPRO annotation.
evidence: The number of unannotated genes is explicitly stated.

claim: The majority of the genes identified in the screen have not previously been linked to Notch.
source: The majority of the genes identified in this screen have not previously been linked to Notch.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation from the screen results.

claim: Only one cell cycle gene (inscuteable) was previously directly linked to Notch among the 31 annotated cell cycle genes identified.
source: For example, analysis of known and predicted interactions using the GeneMania platform between Notch and the 31 annotated cell cycle genes shows that only one (inscuteable, insc) was previously directly linked to Notch (Figure 1C).
evidence: Network analysis results are presented showing prior connections to Notch.

claim: The Exelixis line d10338 is predicted to overexpress Src42A.
source: These two lines were d08184 (predicted to overexpress Eip75EF) and d10338 (predicted to overexpress Src42A).
evidence: The predicted gene affected by the Exelixis insertion is stated.

claim: The combination of d10338 with UAS-Nact results in a strong enhancement of the Nact large eye phenotype.
source: The combination of d10338 with UAS-Nact, under the E1Gal4 driver, results in a strong enhancement (Figure 2A) of the Nact large eye phenotype (Figure 2C).
evidence: The phenotypic enhancement is described and shown in figures.

claim: Outgrowths of eye tissue protruding from the borders of the eye are observed when d10338 is combined with UAS-Nact.
source: We also often observe outgrowths of eye tissue protruding from the borders of the eye (arrow in Figure 2A).
evidence: The phenotype is described and indicated in the figure.

claim: d10338 alone produces smaller eyes than wild-type controls.
source: Notably, d10338 alone produced smaller eyes (Figure 2B) than wild-type controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: The phenotype is described and shown in figures.

claim: Src42ACA causes hyperplastic eye growth in combination with Nact.
source: Indeed, Src42ACA also causes hyperplastic eye growth in combination with Nact (Figure 2E)
evidence: The phenotype is described and shown in the figure.

claim: Src42ACA alone results in reduced eye size.
source: and reduced eye size when expressed on its own (Figure 2F).
evidence: The phenotype is described and shown in the figure.

claim: Gal4-driven expression of d10338 results in upregulation of the Src42A gene product.
source: As expected, Gal4-driven expression of d10338 results in an upregulation of both the Src42A gene product and the active, phosphorylated form of Src in vgGal4/d10338 wing discs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qPCR and immunostaining data are referenced showing increased Src42A expression.

claim: Gal4-driven expression of d10338 results in upregulation of the active, phosphorylated form of Src.
source: As expected, Gal4-driven expression of d10338 results in an upregulation of both the Src42A gene product and the active, phosphorylated form of Src in vgGal4/d10338 wing discs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunostaining data showing phosphorylated Src is referenced.

claim: VgGal4-driven expression of UAS-Nact and UAS-Src42ACA in the wing disc results in a hyperplastic phenotype with a characteristic 'crumpled ball' appearance.
source: VgGal4-driven expression of UAS-Nact and UAS-Src42ACA in the wing disc also resulted in a hyperplastic phenotype; the wing discs are not only overgrown but also noticeably disorganized, with a characteristic 'crumpled ball' phenotype (Figure 2I).
evidence: The phenotype is described and shown in the figure.

claim: Larvae expressing UAS-Nact and UAS-Src42ACA under VgGal4 fail to pupate and develop a 'giant larvae' phenotype.
source: Furthermore, these larvae fail to pupate and develop a 'giant larvae' phenotype.
evidence: The developmental phenotype is explicitly described.

claim: Src42ACA alone causes disorganization but no increase in overall disc size.
source: Src42ACA alone causes disorganization but no increase in overall disc size (Figure 2J)
evidence: The phenotype is described and shown in the figure.

claim: Nact alone causes increased disc size but minimal apparent disorganization.
source: whereas Nact alone causes increased disc size but minimal apparent disorganization (Figure 2K).
evidence: The phenotype is described and shown in the figure.

claim: There are two distinct Src family members in Drosophila, Src42A and Src64B.
source: There are two distinct Src family members in Drosophila, Src42A and Src64B.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila Src genes.

claim: Src42A and Src64B are both widely expressed and may be redundant in many cases.
source: Previous reports have shown that they are both widely expressed and may be redundant in many cases (Takahashi et al., 1996; Tateno et al., 2000; Takahashi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: Src64B synergizes with Nact to produce hyperplastic eyes with outgrowths and overgrown, disorganized wing discs.
source: Consistent with the notion that Src42A and Src64B function similarly, we find that Src64B also interacts with Nact to produce hyperplastic eyes with outgrowths and overgrown, disorganized wing discs (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The phenotype is described and shown in figures.

claim: Coexpression of Nact and Src42ACA in vgGal4 wing discs results in strong, widespread puc-LacZ expression.
source: Coexpression of Nact and Src42ACA in vgGal4 wing discs results in strong, widespread LacZ expression (Figure 2M).
evidence: The reporter assay result is described and shown in the figure.

claim: Nact or Src42ACA alone each induce far weaker, spatially restricted puc-LacZ activation compared to their combination.
source: In contrast, Nact or Src42ACA alone each induced far weaker, spatially restricted puc-LacZ activation (Figure 2N,O).
evidence: The reporter assay results are described and shown in figures.

claim: Coexpression of Nact and Src42ACA causes high levels of MMP1.
source: Coexpression of Nact and Src42ACA caused high levels of both MMP1 and cl-casp3 (Figure 3A,G).
evidence: Immunostaining results are described and shown in figures.

claim: Coexpression of Nact and Src42ACA causes high levels of cleaved caspase 3.
source: Coexpression of Nact and Src42ACA caused high levels of both MMP1 and cl-casp3 (Figure 3A,G).
evidence: Immunostaining results are described and shown in figures.

claim: Nact+Mef2 results in robust MMP1 activation but little to no apoptosis.
source: This is in striking contrast to Nact+Mef2, which results in robust MMP1 activation but little to no apoptosis, consistent with our previous report (Figure 3F,L) (Pallavi et al., 2012).
evidence: The phenotype is described, shown in figures, and compared to previous findings.

claim: BskDN reduces both MMP1 and cleaved caspase 3 to near-wildtype levels in N/Src wing discs.
source: We found that BskDN reduced both MMP1 and cl-casp3 to near-wildtype levels (Figure 3E,K).
evidence: The rescue experiment results are described and shown in figures.

claim: Nact+Src42ACA causes a synergistic downregulation of both egr and wgn.
source: We find that Nact+Src42ACA actually causes a synergistic downregulation of both egr and its receptor wengen (wgn), suggesting that unlike the N/Mef2 synergy, N/Src activates JNK via a TNF-independent mechanism (Figure 3M).
evidence: qPCR results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: N/Src activates JNK via a TNF-independent mechanism.
source: We find that Nact+Src42ACA actually causes a synergistic downregulation of both egr and its receptor wengen (wgn), suggesting that unlike the N/Mef2 synergy, N/Src activates JNK via a TNF-independent mechanism (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is inferred from the downregulation of egr and wgn.

claim: DppGal4-driven Nact+Src42ACA induces MMP1 in the wing disc, and this effect is rescuable by BskDN.
source: Just as with vgGal4, dppGal4-driven Nact+Src42ACA induces MMP1 and cl-casp3 in the wing disc, and this effect is rescuable by BskDN (Figure 4).
evidence: The experimental results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: DppGal4-driven Nact+Src42ACA induces cleaved caspase 3 in the wing disc, and this effect is rescuable by BskDN.
source: Just as with vgGal4, dppGal4-driven Nact+Src42ACA induces MMP1 and cl-casp3 in the wing disc, and this effect is rescuable by BskDN (Figure 4).
evidence: The experimental results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: Some GFP-positive cells in dppGal4-driven experiments do not express MMP1 or cleaved caspase 3, indicating non-cell-autonomous effects.
source: Indeed, we find that some GFP-positive cells, notably those in the far ventral region of the disc, do not obviously express either MMP1 or cl-casp3 (green arrows in Figure 4).
evidence: The observation is described and indicated in the figure.

claim: Some apoptosis is detected in GFP-negative domains of both Nact+Src42ACA and Src42ACA wing discs, suggesting a non-cell-autonomous effect.
source: Additionally, some apoptosis is detected in GFP-negative domains of both Nact+Src42ACA and Src42ACA wing discs (red arrows in Figure 4), suggesting a non-cell-autonomous effect
evidence: The observation is described and indicated in the figure.

claim: Src64B in concert with Nact strongly activates both MMP1 and cleaved caspase 3.
source: These observations were also corroborated by determining that Src64B, in concert with Nact, also strongly activates both MMP1 and cl-casp3 (Figure 4F,L,R,X).
evidence: The experimental results are described and shown in figures.

claim: Src64B appears to induce correspondingly higher levels of MMP1 and lower levels of apoptosis than Src42ACA.
source: Interestingly, it appears to induce correspondingly higher levels of MMP1 and lower levels of apoptosis than Src42ACA
evidence: This is observed from comparing the experimental results.

claim: Notch and Src act together to induce JNK signaling and subsequent downstream consequences such as MMP1 activation and induction of apoptosis.
source: Taken together, these findings reveal that Notch and Src act together to induce JNK signaling and subsequent downstream consequences such as MMP1 activation and induction of apoptosis
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data presented.

claim: JNK activation induced by Notch and Src differs subtly from that induced by Notch and Mef2.
source: but that this JNK activation differs subtly from that induced by Notch and Mef2.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the phenotypes and mechanisms of N/Src and N/Mef2.

claim: Src42A or Src64B alone can generate apparently weaker versions of the N/Src synergistic phenotype.
source: It is noteworthy that Src42A or Src64B alone can often generate apparently weaker versions of the N/Src synergistic phenotype (Figures 2–4).
evidence: This observation is noted from the figures showing Src alone phenotypes.

claim: Notch is endogenously active in both the eye and wing discs during the time when the Src transgenes are expressed.
source: Notch is endogenously active in both the eye and wing discs during the time when the Src transgenes are expressed in our experiments (Johnston and Edgar, 1998; Baonza and Garcia-Bellido, 2000; Baonza and Freeman, 2005; Herranz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: The effects of Src alone are caused by synergy between exogenous Src and endogenous Notch.
source: We therefore suspected that the observed effects of Src alone could be caused by synergy between exogenous Src and endogenous Notch.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that Src alone produces phenotypes similar to N/Src.

claim: The N55e11 heterozygous mutation decreases levels of endogenous Notch in the developing wing.
source: To test this, we used the N55e11 heterozygous mutation to decrease levels of endogenous Notch in the developing wing.
evidence: This is implied by the use of the mutation to test the hypothesis about endogenous Notch.

claim: N55e11/+;vgGal4/UAS-Src64B flies demonstrate reduced lethality compared to FM7C/+;vgGal4/UAS-Src64B siblings.
source: In contrast, N55e11/+;vgGal4/UAS-Src64B siblings demonstrated reduced lethality (n = 126) and fully extended, notched wings similar to the notched wing phenotype of N55e11/+;vgGal4/+ controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The experimental results are described and shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: MMP1 and cleaved caspase 3 induced by Src64B are significantly reduced in N55e11/+;vgGal4/UAS-Src64B wing discs.
source: MMP1 and cl-casp3 induced by Src64B were also significantly reduced in N55e11/+;vgGal4/UAS-Src64B wing discs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: The experimental results are described and shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: When UAS-NRNAi is added to d10338, lethality is largely rescued and the wings form long, thin spikes similar to those generated by NRNAi alone.
source: In contrast, when UAS-NRNAi is added, lethality is largely rescued (n = 67, vs 108 balancer siblings) and the wings form long, thin spikes similar to those generated by NRNAi alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I–K).
evidence: The experimental results are described and shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Nact+Src64B cells show a complete loss of G1 phase.
source: Whereas wild type and Nact cells have 23% and 25% of cells in G1 phase respectively, Nact+Src64B cells showed a complete loss of G1 phase.
evidence: DNA content analysis results are described.

claim: Src64B alone causes a partial loss of G1 phase (4%).
source: Src64B alone caused a partial loss of G1 phase (4%).
evidence: DNA content analysis results are described.

claim: The effect on the cell cycle appears to be dependent on JNK signaling, as blocking JNK with BskDN strongly reverses the G1 bypass.
source: The effect on the cell cycle appears to be dependent on JNK signaling, as blocking JNK with BskDN strongly reversed the G1 bypass (19% of cells in G1).
evidence: DNA content analysis results with BskDN are described.

claim: Src42ACA and d10338 produce cell cycle distribution profiles (2% and 3% in G1 phase respectively) similar to Src64B when coexpressed with Nact.
source: Both Src42A alleles (Src42ACA and d10338) produced cell cycle distribution profiles (2% and 3% in G1 phase respectively) similar to Src64B when coexpressed with Nact.
evidence: DNA content analysis results are described.

claim: Wing disc cells coexpressing Nact and Mef2 display a decreased number of cells in G1 phase (5%).
source: Likewise, wing disc cells coexpressing Nact and Mef2 displayed a decreased number of cells in G1 phase (5%) (Figure 5A).
evidence: DNA content analysis results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: Cells from dppGal4;UAS-GFP wing discs coexpressing Src64B and Nact display a similar, JNK-dependent loss of the G1 peak.
source: Cells from dppGal4;UAS-GFP wing discs, similar to those from vgGal4; UAS-GFP discs, coexpressing Src64B and Nact also displayed a similar, JNK-dependent loss of the G1 peak (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: DNA content analysis results are described and shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Control ZNC cells that are arrested in G1 do not enter S phase and therefore do not incorporate EdU.
source: Control ZNC cells that are arrested in G1 do not enter S phase and therefore do not incorporate EdU (Figure 5E)
evidence: EdU incorporation assay results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: Nact alone causes ZNC expansion and a partially non-cell autonomous increase in EdU incorporation in the dorsal region of the disc.
source: Nact alone causes ZNC expansion and a partially non-cell autonomous increase in EdU incorporation in the dorsal region of the disc (Figure 5D), as previously reported (Go et al., 1998; Johnston and Edgar, 1998; Herranz et al., 2008).
evidence: EdU incorporation assay results are described, shown in the figure, and compared to previous reports.

claim: Discs expressing Nact and d10338 show a reduced ZNC with correspondingly more EdU-labeled cells in the D–V boundary.
source: In contrast, discs expressing Nact and d10338 show a reduced ZNC with correspondingly more EdU-labeled cells in the D–V boundary, and the area of Notch-induced increased proliferation in the dorsal region is expanded, extending all the way down to the ZNC and greatly increasing the size of the dorsal compartment (Figure 5B).
evidence: EdU incorporation assay results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: The cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitor dacapo (dap) blocks G1 to S transition and is important for cell cycle exit in G1.
source: Given that the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitor dacapo (dap) blocks G1 to S transition and is important for cell cycle exit in G1 (de Nooij et al., 1996; Lane et al., 1996)
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: Nact+Src42ACA expression is associated with a downregulation of both Notch-induced and endogenous dap transcription.
source: qPCR reveals that Nact+Src42ACA expression is indeed associated with a downregulation of both Notch-induced and endogenous dap transcription
evidence: qPCR results are described.

claim: Nact+Mef2 reduces dap levels, although to a lesser extent than Nact+Src42ACA.
source: we note that Nact+Mef2 similarly reduced dap levels, although to a lesser extent (Figure 5F).
evidence: qPCR results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: Nact alone activates dap-LacZ.
source: Nact alone activates dap-LacZ
evidence: Reporter assay results are described.

claim: Nact+Src42ACA suppresses not only the Notch-induced increase in dap-LacZ but also the endogenous expression of the reporter.
source: and Nact+Src42ACA suppresses not only this increase but also the endogenous expression of the reporter (Figure 5G,I,J).
evidence: Reporter assay results are described and shown in figures.

claim: Src42ACA alone causes a significant decrease in dap-LacZ reporter expression.
source: Src42ACA alone also causes a significant decrease in reporter expression (Figure 5H).
evidence: Reporter assay results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: N/Src synergy results in bypassing the G1 phase of the cell cycle, likely via the downregulation of the CDK inhibitor dacapo.
source: We conclude that N/Src synergy results in bypassing the G1 phase of the cell cycle, likely via the downregulation of the CDK inhibitor dacapo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on cell cycle and dap expression.

claim: Both Src and Notch individually can activate JAK/STAT.
source: furthermore, both Src and Notch individually can activate JAK/STAT (Tateno et al., 2000; Read et al., 2004; Reynolds-Kenneally and Mlodzik, 2005).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: All three upd genes are strongly upregulated in a synergistic manner by Nact+Src42ACA.
source: We found that all three upd genes were strongly upregulated in a synergistic manner by Nact+Src42ACA
evidence: qPCR results are described.

claim: The upregulation of upd genes by Nact+Src42ACA is largely suppressed by the addition of BskDN, indicating that it is dependent on JNK signals.
source: furthermore, this upregulation was largely suppressed by the addition of BskDN, indicating that it is dependent on JNK signals.
evidence: qPCR results with BskDN are described.

claim: Nact+Mef2 activates the upd ligands, but to a far lesser extent than Nact+Src42ACA.
source: Nact+Mef2 also activated the upd ligands, but to a far lesser extent (Figure 6A).
evidence: qPCR results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: The combination of UAS-Nact and UAS-Src42ACA driven by vgGal4 induces strong upd-LacZ reporter activation compared to either gene alone or controls.
source: An upd-LacZ reporter line reveals similar results, with the combination of UAS-Nact and UAS-Src42ACA driven by vgGal4 inducing strong reporter activation compared to either gene alone or controls expressing vgGal4 alone (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: Reporter assay results are described and shown in figures.

claim: Src42ACA or Nact alone each cause weak 10XSTATGFP activation.
source: We find that, whereas Src42ACA or Nact alone each caused weak 10XSTATGFP activation, the combination of the two resulted in strong reporter activation throughout the disc (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: Reporter assay results are described and shown in figures.

claim: The combination of Src42ACA and Nact results in strong 10XSTATGFP reporter activation throughout the disc.
source: We find that, whereas Src42ACA or Nact alone each caused weak 10XSTATGFP activation, the combination of the two resulted in strong reporter activation throughout the disc (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: Reporter assay results are described and shown in figures.

claim: BskDN reduces 10XSTATGFP reporter activation induced by Nact+Src42ACA.
source: Moreover, consistent with the observation that blocking JNK reduces the expression of the upd genes, BskDN also reduced 10XSTATGFP reporter activation (Figure 6F).
evidence: Reporter assay results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: N/Src synergy results in activation of JAK/STAT signaling by the upregulation of the upd ligands in a JNK-dependent manner.
source: Thus, N/Src synergy results in activation of JAK/STAT signaling by the upregulation of the upd ligands in a JNK-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on upd expression and JAK/STAT activation.

claim: 187 genes were identified as synergistic targets of Nact+Src42ACA, of which 87 were downregulated and 100 were upregulated.
source: By these criteria, we identified 187 genes, of which 87 were downregulated and 100 were upregulated
evidence: RNA-seq analysis results are described.

claim: The effects on expression of 130 of the 187 synergistic target genes were reversed by BskDN, indicating their expression is dependent on JNK.
source: the effects on expression of 130 of these genes was reversed by BskDN (Supplementary file 3), consistent with the notion that their expression is dependent on JNK.
evidence: RNA-seq analysis results with BskDN are described.

claim: Of the 187 Drosophila synergistic target genes, 120 have clear human orthologs.
source: We note that of these 187 Drosophila genes, 120 have clear human orthologs (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The number of genes with human orthologs is stated.

claim: 44 of the synergistic target genes were validated with qPCR, and 4/44 were determined to be false positives.
source: We validated 44 of these genes with qPCR; 4/44 were thus determined to be false positives.
evidence: Validation results are described.

claim: Only E(spl)mγ was synergistically upregulated among the E(spl) complex members expressed in the wing disc.
source: However, only E(spl)mγ was synergistically upregulated.
evidence: qPCR results for E(spl) complex members are described.

claim: The other five expressed E(spl) genes (E(spl)m8, E(spl)m3, E(spl)m7, E(spl)mβ, and E(spl)mδ) were upregulated by Nact alone, but this upregulation appeared to be suppressed by the addition of Src.
source: The other five expressed genes in the locus (E(spl)m8, E(spl)m3, E(spl)m7, E(spl)mβ, and E(spl)mδ) were, as expected, upregulated by Nact alone, but, interestingly, this upregulation actually appeared to be suppressed by the addition of Src, sometimes all the way back to WT levels
evidence: qPCR results for E(spl) complex members are described.

claim: BskDN reverses both the N/Src-induced enhancement of E(spl)mγ and the suppression of the other five E(spl) genes.
source: BskDN reversed both the N/Src-induced enhancement of E(spl)mγ (albeit weakly) and the suppression of the other five E(spl) genes (Figure 7A).
evidence: qPCR results with BskDN are described and shown in the figure.

claim: Nact+Mef2 causes suppression of all of the E(spl) genes, including E(spl)mγ.
source: In contrast, Nact+Mef2 caused suppression of all of the E(spl) genes, including E(spl)mγ (Figure 7A).
evidence: qPCR results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: Nact causes an increase in the number of cells that express E(spl)mγ-LacZ.
source: While, as expected, Nact causes an increase in the number of cells that express E(spl)mγ-LacZ, Nact+Src42ACA does not
evidence: Reporter assay results are described.

claim: Nact+Src42ACA does not increase the number of cells that express E(spl)mγ-LacZ.
source: While, as expected, Nact causes an increase in the number of cells that express E(spl)mγ-LacZ, Nact+Src42ACA does not
evidence: Reporter assay results are described.

claim: Src42ACA alone eliminates the endogenous pattern of E(spl)mγ-LacZ, possibly due to cell death.
source: interestingly Src42ACA alone eliminates the endogenous pattern of E(spl)mγ-LacZ, possibly due to cell death (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Reporter assay results are described and shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: E(spl)mγ activation by N/Src may be driven by a genomic region distinct from the 234-bp mγ enhancer region.
source: This observation raises the possibility that E(spl)mγ activation by N/Src is driven by a genomic region distinct from the 234-bp mγ enhancer region.
evidence: This is speculated based on the reporter assay results.

claim: Cut staining is upregulated in a broad swath when Nact alone is driven by vgGal4.
source: As expected, cut staining was upregulated in a broad swath when Nact alone was driven by vgGal4 (Figure 7D).
evidence: Immunostaining results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: Ectopic cut expression appears to be completely absent in Nact+Src42ACA wing discs.
source: Strikingly, this ectopic cut expression appeared to be completely absent in Nact+Src42ACA wing discs (Figure 7B).
evidence: Immunostaining results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: Endogenous cut disappears in both Nact+Src42ACA and Src42ACA wing discs.
source: Furthermore, even endogenous cut disappeared in both Nact+Src42ACA (Figure 7B) and Src42ACA (Figure 7C) wing discs.
evidence: Immunostaining results are described and shown in figures.

claim: Nact+Src42ACA is able to strongly activate the NRE-GFP reporter.
source: We find that Nact+Src42ACA is still able to strongly activate the NRE-GFP reporter (Figure 7F).
evidence: Reporter assay results are described and shown in the figure.

claim: N/Src synergy affects a diverse set of genes largely in a JNK dependent manner, including known Notch targets, which are differentially regulated.
source: These analyses demonstrate that N/Src synergy affects a diverse set of genes largely in a JNK dependent manner, including known Notch targets, which however seem to be differentially regulated.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the transcriptional analysis data.

claim: The genetic circuitry that has evolved to influence the biological outcome of Notch signals is complex.
source: Given that Notch defines an essential, ancient, and highly pleiotropic developmental pathway, it is plausible that the genetic circuitry that has evolved to influence the biological outcome of Notch signals is complex.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle based on the nature of Notch signaling.

claim: N/Src both accesses and interprets JNK signals in a manner distinct from that of N/Mef2.
source: Importantly, however, we demonstrate that N/Src both accesses and interprets JNK signals in a manner distinct from that of N/Mef2.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from comparing N/Src and N/Mef2 mechanisms and phenotypes.

claim: The Exelixis mutant collection disrupts only approximately 53% of the fly genome.
source: It is important to note that our screen is not saturating because the Exelixis mutant collection disrupts only approximately 53% of the fly genome
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the screen.

claim: The true number of genes that can modify Notch-induced proliferation phenotypes is far greater (perhaps at least double) than the 360 identified.
source: In light of the above information, we presume that the true number of genes that can modify Notch-induced proliferation phenotypes is far greater (perhaps at least double) than the 360 we have identified in this work
evidence: This is inferred from the limitations of the screen.

claim: 31 genes identified in the screen are annotated as cell cycle genes, representing a more than twofold enrichment.
source: Most notably, 31 genes are annotated as cell cycle genes, representing a more than twofold enrichment.
evidence: This is stated based on the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes involved in mitosis are highly represented among the screen hits.
source: In particular, genes involved in mitosis are highly represented.
evidence: This is stated based on the analysis of screen hits.

claim: Nanos can directly repress Cyclin B (CycB) in the germline, thereby preventing mitosis.
source: This finding is corroborated by the observation that nanos can directly repress Cyclin B (CycB) in the germline, thereby preventing mitosis (Kadyrova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on a cited previous study.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated colocalization of Notch and c-Src proteins in pancreatic cancer cells, where Src is required for proteolytic activation of Notch.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated colocalization of Notch and c-Src proteins in pancreatic cancer cells, where Src is required for proteolytic activation of Notch (Ma et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated based on a cited previous study.

claim: Notch and the T-cell-specific Src family member Lck colocalize in T cells.
source: and of Notch and the T-cell-specific Src family member Lck in T cells (Sade et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated based on a cited previous study.

claim: A functional relationship between Notch and Src had not been demonstrated prior to this study.
source: but a functional relationship between the two genes had not been demonstrated prior to our study.
evidence: This is stated to highlight the novelty of the current findings.

claim: The major target of the N/Src synergy is the JNK pathway.
source: Given that the majority of N/Src phenotypes and changes in almost 70% of the transcriptional targets can be effectively reversed upon JNK inhibition it seems clear that the major target of the N/Src synergy is the JNK pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from the rescue experiments with BskDN.

claim: N/Mef2 synergy activates JNK via the TNF ligand egr.
source: Our previously reported N/Mef2 synergy activates JNK via the TNF ligand egr (Pallavi et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated based on a previous study by the authors.

claim: N/Src causes a great deal of apoptosis, whereas N/Mef2 does not.
source: Additionally, N/Src causes a great deal of apoptosis, whereas N/Mef2 does not
evidence: This is observed from comparing the experimental results of N/Src and N/Mef2.

claim: Only N/Src is capable of differentially upregulating E(spl)mγ.
source: and only N/Src is capable of differentially upregulating E(spl)mγ.
evidence: This is observed from comparing the experimental results of N/Src and N/Mef2.

claim: The degree of upregulation of JAK/STAT ligands is more than an order of magnitude greater for N/Src vs N/Mef2.
source: Finally, although both combinations activate JAK/STAT ligands, the degree of upregulation is more than an order of magnitude greater for N/Src vs N/Mef2.
evidence: This is observed from comparing the qPCR results for upd genes.

claim: While JNK activation may be a common thread in Notch-related hyperplastic phenotypes, there may be multiple routes through which JNK is activated, and this difference in access may contribute to differential downstream outputs.
source: These observations suggest that while JNK activation may be a common thread in Notch-related hyperplastic phenotypes, there may be multiple routes through which a single pathway (JNK) is activated, and this difference in access may subsequently contribute to differential downstream outputs (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing N/Src and N/Mef2 mechanisms.

claim: The Notch/JNK signaling axis may represent a primary pathway through which the cell can regulate proliferation and affect cell movement.
source: It is worth noting that the Notch/JNK signaling axis may represent a primary pathway through which the cell can not only regulate proliferation but may also affect cell movement.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed phenotypes and literature.

claim: Two groups have recently reported a role for actin polymerization upstream of JNK activation by Src.
source: Two groups have recently reported a role for actin polymerization upstream of JNK activation by Src (Fernandez et al., 2014; Rudrapatna et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated based on cited recent studies.

claim: Increased actin was observed in N/Mef2 tissues.
source: given that we observed increased actin in N/Mef2 tissues (Pallavi et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated based on a previous study by the authors.

claim: The loss of the epithelial polarity gene scribble (scrib) induces JNK activation leading to cell death; however, in the presence of active Notch, scrib mutant cells instead overgrow and become invasive.
source: the loss of the epithelial polarity gene scribble (scrib) induces JNK activation leading to cell death; however, in the presence of active Notch, scrib mutant cells instead overgrow and become invasive (Brumby and Richardson, 2003).
evidence: This is stated based on a cited previous study.

claim: Overexpression of Notch alone causes local expansion of the ZNC and distant hyperproliferation.
source: Overexpression of Notch alone causes local expansion of the ZNC and distant hyperproliferation (Johnston and Edgar, 1998; Herranz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: The combination of Notch and Src leads to loss of the ZNC and expansion of the hyperproliferative zone.
source: However, our data indicate that the combination of Notch and Src actually leads to loss of the ZNC and expansion of the hyperproliferative zone
evidence: This is observed from the EdU incorporation assay results.

claim: Src modulates the activity of Notch to lead to proliferation rather than differentiation.
source: suggesting that Src modulates the activity of Notch in this situation and leads to proliferation rather than differentiation (as is also implied by the loss of cut in the D–V boundary).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed phenotypes.

claim: The differential regulation of the E(spl) complex genes supports the notion that Src modulates the target specificity of Notch.
source: Our observation of differential regulation of the E(spl) complex genes supports the notion that Src modulates the target specificity of Notch.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR and reporter assay results for E(spl) genes.

claim: The NRE-GFP reporter is strongly upregulated by N/Src (similar to Notch alone).
source: The NRE-GFP reporter is strongly upregulated by N/Src (similar to Notch alone)
evidence: Reporter assay results are described.

claim: Whatever leads to suppression of Notch targets in the presence of Src either does not affect Su(H) binding or requires the modulatory action of additional, differentially acting factors.
source: suggesting that whatever leads to suppression of Notch targets in the presence of Src either does not affect Su(H) binding or requires the modulatory action of additional, differentially acting factors.
evidence: This is speculated based on the NRE-GFP reporter results.

claim: The complete loss of the G1 phase of the cell cycle and an immense degree of hyperplasia are among the most striking N/Src phenotypes.
source: Among the most striking N/Src phenotypes are the complete loss of the G1 phase of the cell cycle and an immense degree of hyperplasia.
evidence: This is stated as a key observation from the study.

claim: The downregulation of dap by N/Src and N/Mef2 suggests a potential mechanism for the G1 bypass.
source: Our observation that the cell cycle regulator dap is downregulated by N/Src and N/Mef2 suggests a potential mechanism for the G1 bypass.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR and reporter assay results for dap.

claim: The G1 phase is important during normal development and homeostasis to allow newly-divided cells to increase in size and replenish protein and energy stores.
source: The G1 phase is important during normal development and homeostasis to allow newly-divided cells to increase in size and replenish protein and energy stores
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the cell cycle.

claim: Regulatory checkpoints during G1 control cell fate choices such as the decision to exit the cell cycle and differentiate.
source: additionally, regulatory checkpoints during G1 control cell fate choices such as the decision to exit the cell cycle and differentiate (Lee and Orr-Weaver, 2003; Hindley and Philpott, 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: Dap is a member of the p21/p27 family of Cdk inhibitors.
source: Dap is a member of the p21/p27 family of Cdk inhibitors
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dap.

claim: Dap is required during Drosophila embryogenesis for proper timing of cell cycle exit at G1.
source: and is required during Drosophila embryogenesis for proper timing of cell cycle exit at G1 (de Nooij et al., 1996; Lane et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: Early Drosophila embryos undergo their first 16 cell divisions without G1 or G2, resulting in rapid cell division without a corresponding increase in compartment size.
source: Early Drosophila embryos undergo their first 16 cell divisions without G1 or G2, resulting in rapid cell division without a corresponding increase in compartment size (Lee and Orr-Weaver, 2003).
evidence: This is stated based on a cited previous study.

claim: Hyperplasia of N/Src wing discs is observed, indicating that compartment growth must occur even in the absence of a detectable G1 phase.
source: In contrast, we observe hyperplasia of N/Src wing discs, indicating that compartment growth must occur even in the absence of a detectable G1 phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed phenotype and cell cycle data.

claim: In the case of Ras or Myc overexpression, the other phases of the cell cycle are prolonged to compensate for decreased time in G1, and the overall growth rate also increases.
source: In the case of Ras or Myc overexpression, the other phases of the cell cycle are prolonged to compensate for decreased time in G1, and the overall growth rate also increases (Johnston et al., 1999; Prober and Edgar, 2000, 2002).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: An increase in the percentage of N/Src cells in S phase is observed, suggesting that the lack of G1 is at least partially compensated for by a longer S phase.
source: We do observe an increase in the percentage of N/Src cells in S phase, suggesting that the lack of G1 is at least partially compensated for by a longer S.
evidence: This is inferred from the DNA content analysis results.

claim: The N/Src cell cycle profile, with absent G1 and a high proportion of cells in S phase, is reminiscent of that of mammalian embryonic stem cells (ESCs).
source: The N/Src cell cycle profile, with absent G1 and a high proportion of cells in S phase, is reminiscent of that of mammalian embryonic stem cells (ESCs), which have an abbreviated G1 and longer S
evidence: This is a comparison drawn based on knowledge of ESC cell cycle characteristics.

claim: Recent studies have suggested that the altered cell cycle of ESCs is necessary to maintain pluripotency, although the mechanisms are still unclear.
source: recent studies have suggested that this altered cycle is necessary to maintain pluripotency, although the mechanisms are still unclear (Orford and Scadden, 2008; Hindley and Philpott, 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on cited recent studies.

claim: N/Src synergy may interfere with cell fate determination, conferring pluripotency.
source: Therefore, this raises the very interesting possibility that N/Src synergy may interfere with cell fate determination, conferring pluripotency.
evidence: This is speculated based on the similarity to ESC cell cycle characteristics.

claim: Src42A and Src64B in Drosophila intestinal stem cells (ISCs) could stimulate the expansion of a transit-amplifying population of Notch-positive cells.
source: A recent report found that Src42A and Src64B in Drosophila intestinal stem cells (ISCs) could stimulate the expansion of a transit-amplifying population of Notch-positive cells (Kohlmaier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on a cited recent study.

claim: Src may interact with Notch in the transit-amplifying cell population to induce proliferation.
source: In light of our findings, we suggest that Src may actually interact with Notch in this cell population to induce proliferation.
evidence: This is suggested based on the current findings and the cited study.

claim: Several previous studies have shown that Src acts through JNK to induce invasive phenotypes, including activation of MMP1.
source: Several previous studies have shown that Src acts through JNK to induce invasive phenotypes, including activation of MMP1 (Ma et al., 2014; Rudrapatna et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: The addition of Notch promotes hyperplastic growth while still retaining and perhaps even enhancing Src-driven invasive behavior.
source: Our work suggests that the addition of Notch promotes hyperplastic growth while still retaining and perhaps even enhancing Src-driven invasive behavior.
evidence: This is concluded from the observed phenotypes of N/Src.

claim: Loss of the Src antagonist Csk in the wing disc can induce activation of JNK and JAK/STAT signaling as well as morphological disorganization.
source: Other studies have reported that loss of the Src antagonist Csk in the wing disc can induce activation of JNK and JAK/STAT signaling as well as morphological disorganization (Read et al., 2004; Vidal et al., 2006; Langton et al., 2007; Vidal et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: Csk phenotypes may result from activation of endogenous Src, which then interacts with endogenous Notch.
source: We hypothesize that these Csk phenotypes may result from activation of endogenous Src, which then interacts with endogenous Notch.
evidence: This is hypothesized based on the current findings and previous studies on Csk.

claim: The Src family members Src, Fyn, and Yes in mammals, as well as Src42A and Src64B in Drosophila, are widely, even ubiquitously expressed, and kept in check partly by the similarly widespread expression of Csk.
source: The Src family members Src, Fyn, and Yes in mammals, as well as Src42A and Src64B in Drosophila, are widely, even ubiquitously expressed, and kept in check partly by the similarly widespread expression of Csk (Takahashi et al., 1996; Tateno et al., 2000; Takahashi et al., 2005; Wheeler et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: Notch is expressed in a large number of tissues.
source: Notch is likewise expressed in a large number of tissues (Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 1999; Artavanis-Tsakonas and Muskavitch, 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: Although the activity and levels of both Src and Notch are often increased in cancers, activating mutations in the genes themselves are rare.
source: Interestingly, although the activity and levels of both Src and Notch are often increased in cancers, activating mutations in the genes themselves are rare (Ishizawar and Parsons, 2004; Ranganathan et al., 2011; Louvi and Artavanis-Tsakonas, 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: Synergy between even relatively low levels of active Notch and Src can activate JNK and cause exponentially increased levels of hyperplastic growth and stimulation of oncogenic events.
source: One explanation suggested by our data is that synergy between even relatively low levels of active Notch and Src can activate JNK and cause exponentially increased levels of hyperplastic growth and stimulation of oncogenic events.
evidence: This is suggested based on the current findings.

claim: An inactivating mutation in Csk could have devastating consequences in both development and cancer by triggering a Notch/Src synergistic response.
source: Additionally, an inactivating mutation in Csk could have devastating consequences in both development and cancer by triggering a Notch/Src synergistic response.
evidence: This is speculated based on the current findings and knowledge of Csk function.

claim: Among the human orthologs of N/Src targets, genes involved in metabolism and stress response are both overrepresented.
source: Among the human orthologs of our N/Src targets, genes involved in metabolism and stress response are both overrepresented.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the N/Src target genes.

claim: N/Src cells may have an increased metabolic rate and heightened protection from stress, both of which could contribute to a favorable environment for oncogenesis.
source: Thus these cells may have an increased metabolic rate (which may also explain the observed overgrowth in the absence of G1) and heightened protection from stress, both of which could contribute to a favorable environment for oncogenesis.
evidence: This is speculated based on the types of genes identified as N/Src targets.

claim: Activated Notch could act as a tumor suppressor in v-Src-transformed quail neuroepithelial cells, causing a reversion of the transformed phenotype along with suppression of JNK signaling.
source: An earlier study revealed that activated Notch could act as a tumor suppressor in v-Src-transformed quail neuroepithelial cells, causing a reversion of the transformed phenotype along with suppression of JNK signaling (Mateos et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on a cited previous study.

claim: Notch can act as either an oncogene and a tumor suppressor depending on context.
source: However, Notch can act as either an oncogene and a tumor suppressor depending on context (Lobry et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on a cited previous study.

claim: Context, including other genes that interact with the N/Src axis, is likely to be essential for determining the outcome of N/Src synergy.
source: Here, too, context, including other genes that interact with the N/Src axis, is likely to be essential
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The N/Mef2 and N/Src synergies both activate the same pathway (JNK) but display differences in downstream phenotype, suggesting that it may be possible to identify targeted, refined signatures for different types of Notch, Src, and JNK-related cancers.
source: Our observation that the N/Mef2 and N/Src synergies both activate the same pathway (JNK) but display differences in downstream phenotype suggests that it may be possible to identify targeted, refined signatures for different types of Notch, Src, and JNK-related cancers.
evidence: This is suggested based on the comparison of N/Mef2 and N/Src mechanisms and phenotypes.

claim: It is more often the context-dependent interplay between genes that causes or modulates cancerous growth, rather than single gene mutations.
source: While single gene mutations can occasionally trigger an oncogenic state, it is more often the context-dependent interplay between genes that causes or modulates cancerous growth.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in cancer biology.
